On August 16, 2026, the Hanshin Tigers faced the Hiroshima Toyo Carp at Mazda Stadium.

Hanshin did not wait long to take control.

In the first inning, Teruaki Sato hit a two-run home run to center field. With one powerful swing, he gave Hanshin an early 2–0 lead.

That start made the road clear for Hanshin pitcher Takato Ihara.

Ihara pitched five innings. He allowed only two hits and one run. He gave Hiroshima very few chances and kept Hanshin in front.

diff_entries.canonical_text: For preschool children, screen time is only one part of daily life. A 2026 study published in *Frontiers in Psychology* asks whether it is also connected with the relationship between children and their mothers. The study followed children aged 3 to 6 in Fuyang, Anhui, China. It used 3 surveys, with 4 months between each one. The first survey included 619 children. The final analysis included 532 children, with mothers answering the questionnaires. The researchers measured 2 sides of the parent-child relationship: closeness and conflict. They also measured each child's average daily screen time.

diff_entries.canonical_text: At the same time, some public benches have been changed to limit how people use them. Sloped seats and center armrests can prevent people from lying across a bench. In other cases, benches are removed completely. These choices are often discussed as hostile architecture or defensive architecture. This creates a difficult question: Is a bench only a seat—or is it part of someone's ability to move through the city? A design that blocks one activity may also remove a resting place for someone else. Yet the evidence about the wider harm remains limited. As of March 2020, one article reported that no wide-scale empirical study had measured the effects of hostile architecture on homeless people or other targeted groups.

The other response is restriction. In a report published by *Coffee Intelligence* on April twenty eighth, 2026, The Barn introduced a one-hour laptop limit, or a full laptop ban on certain busy days. At its Neukölln store in Berlin, the café reported that laptop users occupied more than 70 percent of seats for long periods. It also reported a 25 percent loss in sales before the policy change.

The Barn’s founder, Ralf Rüller, said the business wants to offer an excellent coffee experience. At the same time, he recognizes the demand from remote workers who want to work in cafés.

So the debate is not simply about laptops. It is about whether a café treats work as a problem, a compromise, or a planned part of its identity.
